derivations.claim: Pairing the first tensor factor of $\chi(h\otimes f)$ with $x\in H$ gives $\sum f(S(h_1)x h_3)h_2$, because $\Delta_{H^*}^{(2)}f$ evaluates on the three consecutive factors of $S(h_1)x h_3$. This determines $\chi$ uniquely by finite tensor separation.

The unit identities are $\chi(1\otimes f)=f\otimes1$ and $\chi(h\otimes\varepsilon_H)=\varepsilon_H\otimes h$: the first contracts the first and third dual factors by $\varepsilon_H$, and the second uses $\varepsilon_H\circ S=\varepsilon_H$ from [F3] and the two counit identities in [F1].

For $h,k\in H$, the two sides of $\chi(hk\otimes f)=(\operatorname{id}\otimes m_H)(\chi\otimes\operatorname{id})(\operatorname{id}\otimes\chi)(h\otimes k\otimes f)$, paired with $x$, both equal $\sum f(S(k_1)S(h_1)x h_3k_3)h_2k_2$. On the left use $S(h_1k_1)=S(k_1)S(h_1)$ from [F3]; on the right, the successive crossings evaluate $f_1(S(k_1))f_2(S(h_1))f_3(x)f_4(h_3)f_5(k_3)$, which is the same dual coproduct evaluation.

For $f,g\in H^*$, pairing the first tensor factor of the left side of $\chi(h\otimes(f\odot g))=(m_{H^{*\mathrm{op}}}\otimes\operatorname{id})(\operatorname{id}\otimes\chi)(\chi\otimes\operatorname{id})(h\otimes f\otimes g)$ with $x$ gives the $H$-valued expression $\sum (g*f)(S(h_1)x h_3)h_2$; the $h_2$ factor remains from $\chi$. Since $\Delta(S(h_1)x h_3)=\sum S(h_2)x_1h_4\otimes S(h_1)x_2h_5$ by [F3] and multiplicativity of $\Delta$, this is $\sum g(S(h_2)x_1h_4)f(S(h_1)x_2h_5)h_3$, which is also the result of the two successive crossings on the right.

Write $\chi(h,b)=\sum b_1\otimes h_1$, $\chi(k,c)=\sum c_1\otimes k_1$, and, for each such term, $\chi(h_1,c_1)=\sum c_2\otimes h_2$. Starting with $(a\otimes h),(b\otimes k),(c\otimes l)$, the left association first crosses $h$ past $b$, then crosses the product $h_1k$ past $c$; the $H$ distributive law of step 1.3 expands that second crossing as first crossing $k$ past $c$, then $h_1$ past the resulting $c_1$. It therefore gives $\sum a b_1 c_2\otimes h_2k_1l$. The right association first crosses $k$ past $c$, then crosses $h$ past the product $bc_1$; the $H^{*\mathrm{op}}$ distributive law of step 1.4 expands that crossing as first crossing $h$ past $b$, then $h_1$ past $c_1$, giving the same sum. Associativity of both factor products follows for $H$ from [F1] and for $H^{*\mathrm{op}}$ from [F4]. Thus the associations agree on simple tensors and, by multilinearity, everywhere. The unit identities of step 1.2 make $\varepsilon_H\otimes1_H$ a two-sided unit.

The maps $f\mapsto f\otimes1_H$ and $h\mapsto\varepsilon_H\otimes h$ preserve products by step 1.2 and the defining multiplication. They are injective because applying $\operatorname{id}_{H^*}\otimes\varepsilon_H$ or $\varepsilon_{H^*}\otimes\operatorname{id}_H$ recovers the input; $\varepsilon_H(1_H)=1$.

derivations.claim: The dual coproduct is coassociative because for all $x,y,z\in H$, both iterated coproducts of $f$ evaluate to $f((xy)z)=f(x(yz))$, and its counit is $f\mapsto f(1_H)$; these are also the dual coalgebra maps in [F3]. The tensor coalgebra formula for $\Delta_D$ is therefore coassociative with counit $\varepsilon_D$.

By [F3], the dual Hopf algebra has antipode $S^*(f)=f\circ S$. Since $S$ is bijective, $S^*$ is bijective with inverse $\bar f=f\circ S^{-1}$. The same coproduct makes the opposite product a bialgebra: $\Delta(f\odot g)=\Delta(g*f)=\Delta(g)\Delta(f)=\sum(g_1*f_1)\otimes(g_2*f_2)=\sum(f_1\odot g_1)\otimes(f_2\odot g_2)$. The opposite unit is still $\varepsilon_H$, and $\Delta(\varepsilon_H)=\varepsilon_H\otimes\varepsilon_H$ because $\varepsilon_H(xy)=\varepsilon_H(x)\varepsilon_H(y)$; its counit $f\mapsto f(1_H)$ is multiplicative for $\odot$ since $(f\odot g)(1_H)=(g*f)(1_H)=g(1_H)f(1_H)=f(1_H)g(1_H)$ using $\Delta_H(1_H)=1_H\otimes1_H$. Pairing the two proposed antipode products with $x\in H$ gives $\sum(\bar f_1\odot f_2)(x)=f(S^{-1}(x_2)x_1)=\varepsilon(x)f(1_H)$ and $\sum(f_1\odot\bar f_2)(x)=f(x_2S^{-1}(x_1))=\varepsilon(x)f(1_H)$, using the inverse antipode identities obtained by applying $S^{-1}$ to the equations in [F6] and reversing products by [F4]. Thus $\bar f$ is the antipode of $H^{*\mathrm{op}}$. The tensor coalgebra restricts to these Hopf structures on the two embedded factors.

Define $\psi:H^*\otimes H\to H\otimes H^*$ by $\psi(f\otimes h)=\sum f_1(h_1)f_3(S(h_3))h_2\otimes f_2$. Pairing the dual factor of $\chi\psi(f\otimes h)$ with $x$ gives $\sum f(h_1S(h_2)x h_4S(h_5))h_3=f(x)h$, by the two contractions $h_1S(h_2)=\varepsilon(h)1$ and $h_4S(h_5)=\varepsilon(h)1$. Pairing the dual factor of $\psi\chi(h\otimes f)$ with $x$ gives $\sum f(S(h_1)h_2xS(h_4)h_5)h_3=f(x)h$ by the other two antipode contractions. Finite dual separation [F2] proves $\psi=\chi^{-1}$; equivalently, the inverse crossing relation is $fh=\sum f_1(h_1)f_3(S(h_3))h_2f_2$.

The coproduct is multiplicative on each embedded factor by step 1.2 and the bialgebra equations [F1]. For the mixed crossing, applying $\langle -,x\rangle\otimes\operatorname{id}_H\otimes\langle -,y\rangle\otimes\operatorname{id}_H$ to $\Delta_D(hf)$ and expanding $hf$ gives $\sum f(S(h_1)xyh_4)h_2\otimes h_3$. Applying the same evaluation to $\Delta_D(h)\Delta_D(f)=\sum(h_1f_1)\otimes(h_2f_2)$ and expanding both crossings gives $\sum f(S(h_1)x h_3S(h_4)y h_6)h_2\otimes h_5$. The antipode identity [F6] contracts the adjacent factors $h_3S(h_4)$, leaving $\sum f(S(h_1)xyh_4)h_2\otimes h_3$, the same tensor. By [F2], finite dual evaluations separate tensors, so $\Delta_D(hf)=\Delta_D(h)\Delta_D(f)$.

The map $S_D(fh)=S(h)\bar f$ reverses products on each embedded factor. Applying the inverse crossing of step 1.3 to $\bar f\otimes S(h)$, and using the anti-multiplicative and anti-comultiplicative identities [F4] together with $\bar f=f\circ S^{-1}$, gives $\bar fS(h)=\sum f_1(S(h_1))f_3(h_3)S(h_2)\bar f_2$. This is exactly the reversal of the defining crossing $hf=\sum f_1(S(h_1))f_3(h_3)f_2h_2$. Hence $S_D$ reverses the mixed relation and is an anti-algebra map on the crossed product.

For simple normal tensors $fh$ and $gk$, the product is $f(hg)k$ by [L2]. The defining tensor coalgebra formula gives $\Delta_D(f(hg)k)=\Delta_D(f)\Delta_D(hg)\Delta_D(k)$, because each displayed term is in normal order. The mixed calculation of step 2.1 gives $\Delta_D(hg)=\Delta_D(h)\Delta_D(g)$, and the factor restrictions of step 1.2 give the remaining products. Hence $\Delta_D((fh)(gk))=\Delta_D(fh)\Delta_D(gk)$; linearity proves multiplicativity on all of $D(H)$.

Applying $\varepsilon_D$ to the crossing gives $\sum f_1(S(h_1))f_2(1_H)f_3(h_3)\varepsilon_H(h_2)=\sum f(S(h_1)h_3)\varepsilon_H(h_2)=f(1_H)\varepsilon_H(h)$: the dual coproduct combines the first three evaluations, and applying $\operatorname{id}\otimes\varepsilon\otimes\operatorname{id}$ to $\Delta^{(2)}(h)$ gives $\Delta(h)$ before the antipode contraction [F6]. Thus the counit is multiplicative on the crossing and on both factors; the normal-product calculation of step 3.1 makes it multiplicative on all products. Also $\Delta_D(1_D)=1_D\otimes1_D$, since $\Delta_{H^*}(\varepsilon_H)=\varepsilon_H\otimes\varepsilon_H$ and $\Delta_H(1_H)=1_H\otimes1_H$, and $\varepsilon_D(1_D)=1$. Therefore $D(H)$ is a bialgebra.

For $\Delta_D(fh)=\sum f_1h_1\otimes f_2h_2$, the left antipode contraction is $\sum S(h_1)(\bar f_1\odot f_2)h_2$. By step 1.2 the dual factor contracts to $f(1_H)\varepsilon_H$, and the remaining $S(h_1)h_2$ contracts to $\varepsilon_H(h)1_D$ by [F6]. The right contraction is $\sum f_1h_1S(h_2)\bar f_2$; first contract $h_1S(h_2)$ by [F6] and then use the other dual antipode identity of step 1.2. Both sides equal $f(1_H)\varepsilon_H(h)1_D=\varepsilon_D(fh)1_D$. Thus $S_D$ is an antipode.

derivations.claim: Every linear functional on the free vector space $kG$ is determined by arbitrary values on the basis $G$, so $H^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(H,k)$ identifies with all functions $G\to k$. The standard maps $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$, $\varepsilon(g)=1$ and $S(g)=g^{-1}$ make $kG$ a Hopf algebra: the coproduct is multiplicative on basis products, coassociative and counital on each group element, and the two antipode products equal $e$. Multiplication $\mu:H\otimes H\to H$ therefore has transpose $\mu^*:H^*\to(H\otimes H)^*$, and $\mu^*(\delta_e)(a,b)=\delta_e(ab)$.

Suppose $\mu^*(\delta_e)$ came from a tensor $\sum_{i=1}^n F_i\otimes G_i\in H^*\otimes H^*$. For each fixed $a\in G$, its row function of $b$ would be $\sum_{i=1}^nF_i(a)G_i(b)$, hence all row functions would lie in the finite-dimensional span of $G_1,\ldots,G_n$.

The actual row at $a$ is $b\mapsto\delta_e(ab)=\mathbf1_{b=a^{-1}}$, the point mass at $a^{-1}$. As $a$ ranges over infinite $G$, these are infinitely many distinct point masses; any finite subfamily is linearly independent by evaluation at its respective support point. Their span is therefore infinite-dimensional, contradicting step 1.2. Thus $\mu^*(\delta_e)\notin H^*\otimes H^*$ and the asserted full-dual coproduct does not exist in the algebraic tensor category. This does not rule out the restricted dual $H^\circ$ of [F2].
